description: A three-panel composite figure mixing one tensile curve with two literature-comparison property maps. (a) Engineering stress-strain plot: x-axis "Engineering strain (%)" 0-30 in 5 % steps, y-axis "Engineering stress (MPa)" 0-700 in 100 MPa steps, with three labelled curves — red "Our LDS", which rises steeply, peaks just below the 700 MPa gridline at roughly 13-15 % strain and ends abruptly; orange "Fe-TiB2 steel", peaking between the 500 and 600 MPa gridlines near 10 % strain and ending near 15 %; and black "IF steel", lowest in stress (plateau between 300 and 400 MPa) but most ductile, extending to about 29 % strain. (b) Property map of "Uniform Elongation (%)" (0-30) versus "SYS (MPa g⁻¹ cm³)" (20-200), overlaid with several coloured shaded ellipses of literature data and marker symbols (no visible legend), a red star labelled "Our LDS" near UE ≈ 13 at SYS between the 60 and 80 gridlines, a black star "IF steel" at the highest UE with the lowest SYS, and an arrow to "Fe-TiB2 steel". (c) Property map of "SYS × UE (MPa g⁻¹ cm³)" (0-22) versus "Specific modulus (GPa g⁻¹ cm³)" (20-36) with a dashed boundary line; the red star "Our LDS" lies at the highest specific modulus among the shown steels (near the caption-stated 32.7 GPa g⁻¹ cm³) with SYS × UE around 9-10, the black star "IF steel" at lower SYS × UE, and orange "Fe-TiB2 steel" furthest right. Together the panels argue the present LDS combines a strength-ductility balance competitive with ceramic-reinforced and Al-added lightweight steels while keeping a high specific modulus.

subfigures.description: Engineering stress-strain curves, axes Engineering strain (%) 0-30 and Engineering stress (MPa) 0-700. Three labelled curves: red 'Our LDS' (highest stress, peaks just under 700 MPa, ends ~13-15 % strain), orange 'Fe-TiB2 steel' (peaks between 500 and 600 MPa, ends ~15 %), black 'IF steel' (plateau between 300 and 400 MPa, elongates to ~29 %).

Property map: Uniform Elongation (%) versus SYS (MPa g⁻¹ cm³), with multiple coloured shaded ellipse clusters of literature data and unlabelled marker symbols. Red star 'Our LDS' sits near UE ≈ 13 at SYS ~70; black star 'IF steel' at highest UE (~22-25) and lowest SYS (~30); 'Fe-TiB2 steel' indicated by an arrow into an orange data cluster at intermediate SYS.

Property map: SYS × UE (MPa g⁻¹ cm³) versus Specific modulus (GPa g⁻¹ cm³), with a dashed curve separating data populations. Red star 'Our LDS' at the highest specific modulus (~32-33 GPa g⁻¹ cm³) with SYS × UE ~9-10; black star 'IF steel' at specific modulus ~26.5 with SYS × UE ~5-6; orange arrow points to 'Fe-TiB2 steel' at the far right (specific modulus ~35). No legend key for the coloured regions.

observations.observation: Panel (a) plots engineering stress (MPa) versus engineering strain (%) for three samples labelled in colour: 'Our LDS' (red), 'Fe-TiB2 steel' (orange) and 'IF steel' (black).
The red 'Our LDS' curve in (a) reaches the highest stress level, peaking just below the 700 MPa gridline and terminating at roughly 13-15 % strain.
The orange 'Fe-TiB2 steel' curve in (a) peaks between the 500 and 600 MPa gridlines, below the present steel but above the IF steel.
The black 'IF steel' curve in (a) shows the lowest flow stress (plateau between the 300 and 400 MPa gridlines) but the largest elongation, extending to about 29 % strain.

Panel (b) maps Uniform Elongation (%) against SYS (MPa g⁻¹ cm³) with a red star labelled 'Our LDS', a black star 'IF steel' at high UE/low SYS, and an arrow to 'Fe-TiB2 steel'; several coloured shaded regions group literature data points whose individual symbols carry no visible legend.

Panel (c) maps SYS × UE (MPa g⁻¹ cm³) against Specific modulus (GPa g⁻¹ cm³), with a dashed boundary curve; the red 'Our LDS' star lies at the highest specific modulus of the labelled steels (~32-33 GPa g⁻¹ cm³) with SYS × UE around 9-10.

The caption states that (a) compares the present steel with conventional Fe-TiB steel and interstitial-free steel, (b) compares uniform elongation (UE) with specific yield strength (SYS), and (c) compares specific Young's modulus with the product of SYS and UE.
The citing text reports the present steel's yield strength of 503 MPa and ultimate tensile strength of 672 MPa, i.e. 22 % and 30 % above the Fe-TiB2 steel (sigma_y 389 MPa and sigma_u ~549 MPa).
The citing text reports a uniform elongation of 13 % for the present steel versus 11 % for the existing Fe-TiB2 steel, indicating no ductility loss with the strength increase.
The citing text reports the present steel's density of 6.88 g cm⁻³, Young's modulus of 225 GPa, specific modulus of 32.7 GPa g⁻¹ cm³, SYS of 73.1 MPa g⁻¹ cm³ and SUTS of 97.7 MPa g⁻¹ cm³.

The citing text states that the present steel's data point represents one of the optimal mechanical properties in the SYS-UE space of Fig. 3(b), and that its SYS × UE lies among existing ceramic-reinforcement steels while maintaining a high specific modulus in Fig. 3(c).
No numeric data labels are printed on any of the three panels; values are only read from axis gridlines, so the star coordinates in (b) and (c) cannot be read exactly.
